name: Abesabesi

catalog_citation: Lau, Jonas. 2021. A Digital Reference Grammar of Abesabesi: Documentation, Description and the Development of a Digital Grammar Format. PhD thesis, Universitaet zu Koeln. kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/35719 (389 pp.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.1.5 Tonology, p. 65 (p. 65); typological sketch Sec. 2.1.8 (the text); language identity Sec. 1 (the text)
catalog_quote: Abesabesi has three register tones: a high tone (H) (marked with an acute accent), a mid tone (M) (not marked on vowels) and a low tone (L) (marked with a grave accent). ... The low tone has three different allotones. Following an M, it is produced as a low register tone (see Figure 3.1). Following an H, it is produced as a falling tone, usually starting at a higher pitch than the preceding H (see Figure 3.2). Being the last low tone after one or more consecutive low tones at the end of an utterance, it is produced as an extra low tone (XL) (see Figure 3.3). ... The tone-bearing unit (TBU) is the mora. Light syllables bear one tone, and heavy syllables with long vowels, two vowels, or coda consonants can bear two tones. However, only /j/ and nasal consonants can bear a tone in coda position. The tone borne by a coda consonant can only be L.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (three register tones H/M/L, TBU = mora, downstep; no word-stress rule stated) rests on a 2021 fieldwork reference grammar that Glottolog ranks as the language's most extensive description, held locally with the deciding passage confirmed verbatim at Sec. 3.1.5, pp. 65-66 (minor locator refinement: the TBU sentences are on p. 66, not 65). A a full-text search for stress/accent confirms the grammar contains no stress/accent statement. All other known descriptive works are 1980s Ilorin student essays on single dialects or Agoyi's vowel-harmony studies, none of which is a prosody source likely to override Lau. no reclassification or re-read needed; at most add 'pp. 65-66' to the locator.

sources.citation: Fáladé, Ọpéyemí Williams. 2023. Floating Tone in Èsùkù. LingLit Journal: Scientific Journal for Linguistics and Literature 4(2): 79-88. doi:10.33258/linglit.v4i2.920
sources.tag: likely states tone; not yet obtained
sources.note: First-hand autosegmental study of floating tones in the Èsùkù dialect: a floating High tone functions as genitive marker in N1-N2 constructions (alongside segmental /ɔní-/) and marks completed action in declaratives; the floating H docks on the final vowel of N1 giving a contour that simplifies to level H; V2 elision in V1#V2 genitive contexts. Presupposes the H/M/L register system; grammatical-tone detail for a dialect other than Lau's Ìkáràm base. Author states no previous tone work on Esuku exists.
